2.1 Nesting tabs
The code for the producing nested tabs with a loop is illustrated below.
Note the lower level header is exactly one level lower than the top header.
Note the ::: {.panel-tabset} / ::: system is for .qmd files only, with .Rmd files you simply write ## {.tabset} after the higher level header, and it cuts out after you write another header of that level.
The code here is visible only because I’ve duplicated it outside the {r} chunk so it unevaluated, usually it is invisible.

2.1.2 Applying to ggplot
The only real change from the table version is that you assign the plot to p and call print(p) — the same rule applies as with kable(): inside a loop, ggplot objects must be explicitly printed or knitr drops them silently.
Mixing tables and plots — since both print(knitr::kable(…)) and print(p) work inside the same results=‘asis’ loop, you can easily render a plot and a summary table per tab just by calling both prints before the closing cat(“”).

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.1 Overview
This document covers data masking and tidy evaluation in R — core concepts in the tidyverse, particularly in dplyr, ggplot2, and rlang. It also flags one factual error found in the original source material.
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.2 1. Data Masking
Data masking allows you to refer to columns in a data frame directly, without the df$ prefix.

3.2.1 Base R (without masking)

df <- data.frame(age = sample(1:100, 100, replace = TRUE))
mean(df$age)

[1] 49.89




3.2.2 With data masking (dplyr)

library(tidyverse)

df %>% summarise(mean_age = mean(age))
##   mean_age
## 1    49.89

Here, age is resolved from within df — no df$ needed.


3.2.3 Why “masking”?
When dplyr evaluates age, it first looks inside the data frame. If not found there, it falls back to the global environment. This temporary priority is what “masks” the outer scope.


3.2.4 Packages that use data masking

dplyr: filter(), mutate(), summarise()
ggplot2: aes(x = age, y = score)
rlang: provides the underlying tools for programming with masking
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.3 2. enquo() — Capturing a Single Variable
enquo() captures a function argument as a quosure — a quoted expression bundled with its environment. This lets you delay evaluation until you’re inside a tidy context.

3.3.1 Without enquo() — Broken

my_filter <- function(data, column, value) {
  data %>% filter(column > value)  # column is not found in the data
}

my_filter(df, age, 25)

Error in `filter()`:
ℹ In argument: `column > value`.
Caused by error:
! object 'age' not found




3.3.2 With enquo() — Works

my_filter <- function(data, column, value) {
  col_quo <- enquo(column)
  data %>% filter(!!col_quo > value)
}

df <- tibble(age = c(20, 30, 40))
my_filter(df, age, 25)

# A tibble: 2 × 1
    age
  <dbl>
1    30
2    40


enquo(column) captures age as a quosure; !!col_quo unquotes it (injects it) inside filter().


3.3.3 Related functions



Function
Purpose




enquo()
Capture one argument as a quosure


enquos()
Capture multiple arguments as quosures


quo()
Manually create a quosure


!!
Unquote a single quosure


!!!
Splice a list of quosures


{ }
Shorthand for enquo() + !! (preferred)
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.4 3. {{ }} — The Modern Shorthand
{{ var }} combines enquo() and !! in one clean step. Prefer it for single arguments in most everyday functions.

library(dplyr)

group_and_summarise <- function(data, group_col, summary_col) {
  data %>%
    group_by({{ group_col }}) %>%
    summarise(mean_val = mean({{ summary_col }}, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
}

df <- tibble(
  gender = c("M", "F", "M", "F"),
  score  = c(85, 90, 88, 95)
)

group_and_summarise(df, gender, score)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  gender mean_val
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 F          92.5
2 M          86.5



Limitation: {{ }} handles one variable at a time. For multiple grouping variables, use enquos() + !!! instead.
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.5 4. enquos() — Capturing Multiple Variables
enquos(...) captures any number of arguments as a list of quosures. Use !!! to splice them back into tidyverse functions.

library(dplyr)
library(rlang)


Attaching package: 'rlang'


The following objects are masked from 'package:purrr':

    %@%, flatten, flatten_chr, flatten_dbl, flatten_int, flatten_lgl,
    flatten_raw, invoke, splice

group_and_summarise_multi <- function(data, ..., summary_var) {
  group_vars   <- enquos(...)
  summary_quo  <- enquo(summary_var)

  data %>%
    group_by(!!!group_vars) %>%
    summarise(mean_val = mean(!!summary_quo, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
}

df <- tibble(
  gender = c("M", "F", "M"),
  city   = c("A", "A", "B"),
  score  = c(85, 90, 88)
)

group_and_summarise_multi(df, gender, city, summary_var = score)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  gender city  mean_val
  <chr>  <chr>    <dbl>
1 F      A           90
2 M      A           85
3 M      B           88


enquos() also works with a single variable, but enquo() or { } is simpler when you only need one.
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.6 5. !! and !!! Explained

3.6.1 !! — Unquote (single)
Injects one captured quosure into an expression.

summarise_one <- function(data, column) {
  col <- enquo(column)
  data %>% summarise(mean_val = mean(!!col))
}



3.6.2 !!! — Splice (multiple)
Expands a list of quosures into separate arguments — equivalent to writing them out individually.

group_multi <- function(data, ...) {
  group_vars <- enquos(...)

  data %>%
    group_by(!!!group_vars) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

Analogy: if group_vars holds quo(gender) and quo(city), then !!!group_vars inside group_by() becomes group_by(gender, city).
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.7 6. String-Based Column Selection
When column names are supplied as character strings (common in Shiny or programmatically generated pipelines), use all_of() and .data[[]].

library(dplyr)

group_and_summarise_str <- function(data, group_cols, summary_col) {
  data %>%
    group_by(across(all_of(group_cols))) %>%
    summarise(mean_val = mean(.data[[summary_col]], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
}

df <- tibble(
  gender = c("M", "F", "M", "F"),
  city   = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  score  = c(85, 90, 88, 95)
)

group_and_summarise_str(df, group_cols = c("gender", "city"), summary_col = "score")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  gender city  mean_val
  <chr>  <chr>    <dbl>
1 F      A           90
2 F      B           95
3 M      A           85
4 M      B           88
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.8 7. sym() — Creating Symbols from Strings
sym() from rlang converts a character string into a symbol that can be unquoted with !! inside tidy verbs.

library(rlang)
library(dplyr)

my_summarise <- function(data, col_name) {
  sym_col <- sym(col_name)
  data %>%
    summarise(avg = mean(!!sym_col, na.rm = TRUE))
}

df <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, 3))
my_summarise(df, "x")

# A tibble: 1 × 1
    avg
  <dbl>
1     2



3.8.1 Comparison of symbol-related tools








Function
Purpose
Use with




sym("x")
String → symbol (rlang, tidy-friendly)
!!sym(...)


as.symbol("x")
String → symbol (base R)
Base R eval()


enquo(x)
Capture argument as quosure
!! in tidy verbs


{ x }
Shorthand capture + unquote
Inside functions
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.9 Symbols
A symbol (also called a name) is one of R’s basic building blocks.
It represents the name of an object rather than its value.
When you type age in R, you’re using a symbol — R looks it up and returns whatever value is bound to that name.
A symbol is the thing before the lookup happens.

3.9.1 Creating symbols explicitly
Normally R creates symbols implicitly, but you can create one directly from a string:

as.symbol("x")   # base R — correct

x

as.name("x")     # base R — also correct, identical to as.symbol()

x


These are base R functions. They’re useful when you have a column name as a string and need to turn it into something R can evaluate as code. You can confirm what you get back:

x <- as.symbol("age")
typeof(x)   # "symbol"

[1] "symbol"

class(x)    # "name"

[1] "name"


Note that x now holds the symbol age, not the string “age”, and not any value called age. It’s a reference waiting to be evaluated.
Why does this matter for tidy evaluation?
Inside dplyr verbs, R expects column references to be symbols, not strings. So if you have a column name stored as a string and want to use it programmatically, you need to convert it first:

df <- data.frame(age = sample(1:100, 100, replace = TRUE))

col_name <- "age"

# This won't work — dplyr sees the string "age", not the column
df %>% summarise(mean(col_name))

Warning: There was 1 warning in `summarise()`.
ℹ In argument: `mean(col_name)`.
Caused by warning in `mean.default()`:
! argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA


  mean(col_name)
1             NA

# Convert to symbol first, then unquote with !!
col_sym <- as.symbol(col_name)
df %>% summarise(mean(!!col_sym))

  mean(age)
1     47.27





3.9.2 tidyr symbols
rlang::sym() — the tidyverse version rlang::sym() does exactly the same thing as as.symbol(), but is designed to work smoothly within tidy evaluation:

rlang::sym("x")  # tidyverse — correct and preferred

x




col_sym <- sym("age")     # same result as as.symbol("age")
df %>% summarise(mean(!!col_sym, na.rm = TRUE))

  mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)
1                   47.27


Prefer sym() in tidyverse code for two reasons. First, it integrates naturally with !! and the rest of the rlang toolkit. Second, there is a plural form syms() that converts a list of strings into a list of symbols, ready to be spliced with !!!:

df <- tibble(
  gender = c("M", "F", "M", "F"),
  city   = c("A", "A", "B", "B"),
  score  = c(85, 90, 88, 95)
)

cols <- syms(c("gender", "score", "city"))

df %>% select(!!!cols)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  gender score city 
  <chr>  <dbl> <chr>
1 M         85 A    
2 F         90 A    
3 M         88 B    
4 F         95 B    


This is particularly useful when column names come from a character vector — for example, from a config file, user input, or the result of names().
crumbs: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.10 8. Argument Validation: match.arg() and stop()
When writing functions that accept restricted choices or require specific inputs, validate arguments early and fail with a clear, informative error.

3.10.1 match.arg() — restricting to an allowed set
Declare the default as a vector of options and match.arg() handles both validation and the default (first element) automatically. Partial matching is also supported.

summarise_col <- function(data, col_name, fn = c("mean", "median", "sum")) {
  fn <- match.arg(fn)

  result <- switch(fn,
    mean   = mean(data[[col_name]],   na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(data[[col_name]], na.rm = TRUE),
    sum    = sum(data[[col_name]],    na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  tibble(stat = fn, value = result)
}

summarise_col(df, "score")           # uses "mean" by default

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  stat  value
  <chr> <dbl>
1 mean   89.5

summarise_col(df, "score", "median") # explicit choice

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  stat   value
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 median    89

summarise_col(df, "score", "med")    # partial matching — also works

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  stat   value
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 median    89

summarise_col(df, "score", "non_Stat_value")

Error in match.arg(fn): 'arg' should be one of "mean", "median", "sum"




3.10.2 stop() — raising custom errors
Use stop() for conditions match.arg() can’t handle, such as checking that a column exists or is the right type. Place these checks at the top of the function so the user gets a clear message immediately rather than a cryptic error from inside a tidy verb.

summarise_col_safe <- function(data, col_name, fn = c("mean", "median", "sum")) {
  if (!col_name %in% names(data)) {
    stop("Column '", col_name, "' not found in data. ",
         "Available columns: ", paste(names(data), collapse = ", "))
  }

  if (!is.numeric(data[[col_name]])) {
    stop("Column '", col_name, "' must be numeric, but is ",
         class(data[[col_name]]), ".")
  }

  fn <- match.arg(fn)
  # ... rest of function
  
  return("met conditions")
  
}

df$city # non numeric

[1] "A" "A" "B" "B"

summarise_col_safe(df, "city")

Error in summarise_col_safe(df, "city"): Column 'city' must be numeric, but is character.

names(df) # Variable name not present

[1] "gender" "city"   "score" 

summarise_col_safe(df, "miss_var")

Error in summarise_col_safe(df, "miss_var"): Column 'miss_var' not found in data. Available columns: gender, city, score

# numeric, non-missing var
df$score

[1] 85 90 88 95

summarise_col_safe(df, "score") 

[1] "met conditions"




3.10.3 stopifnot() — compact assertions
For simple yes/no checks, stopifnot() is more concise. The named form ("message" = expression) produces readable errors and is available from R 4.0.0 onwards.
This checks that

variable is a string, and length = 1,
column in data,
column is numeric.


summarise_col_assert <- function(data, col_name, fn = c("mean", "median", "sum")) {
  stopifnot(
    "col_name must be a single string" = is.character(col_name) && length(col_name) == 1,
    "col_name must exist in data"      = col_name %in% names(data),
    "column must be numeric"           = is.numeric(data[[col_name]])
  )

  fn <- match.arg(fn)
  # ... rest of function
  
  return("Met conditions")
}

df$city # non numeric

[1] "A" "A" "B" "B"

summarise_col_assert(df, "city")

Error in summarise_col_assert(df, "city"): column must be numeric

names(df) # Variable name not present

[1] "gender" "city"   "score" 

summarise_col_assert(df, "miss_var")

Error in summarise_col_assert(df, "miss_var"): col_name must exist in data

# Length > 1
summarise_col_assert(df, c("miss_var", "Score"))

Error in summarise_col_assert(df, c("miss_var", "Score")): col_name must be a single string

# numeric, non-missing var
df$score

[1] 85 90 88 95

summarise_col_assert(df, "score") 

[1] "Met conditions"




3.10.4 rlang::abort() — tidyverse-style errors
Preferred over stop() when writing functions that integrate closely with the tidyverse. Produces structured conditions with a catchable class and better stack traces.
Need look at more.

summarise_col_tidy <- function(data, col_name, fn = c("mean", "median", "sum")) {
  if (!col_name %in% names(data)) {
    abort(
      paste0("Column '", col_name, "' not found in data."),
      class = "col_not_found_error",
      col   = col_name
    )
  }

  fn <- match.arg(fn)
  # ... rest of function
}

# Length > 1
summarise_col_tidy(df, c("miss_var", "score"))

Error in if (!col_name %in% names(data)) {: the condition has length > 1


The class argument lets callers catch specific error types with tryCatch(), which is especially useful in package development or Shiny apps.


3.10.5 Summary of validation tools







Tool
Best for




match.arg()
Restricting a character arg to a fixed set of values


stop()
Custom error messages with flexible conditions


stopifnot()
Compact multi-condition assertions (R 4.0.0+)


rlang::abort()
Structured, classable errors for package/tidy code

title: 3  Tidy Evaluation in R: Data Masking & Non-Standard Evaluation
text:
3.11 Summary







Goal
Tool




Use column name in a function (1 var)
{ var } or enquo()


Use column names in a function (n vars)
enquos(...) + !!!


Column name as a string
sym() + !!


Multiple string-based column names
all_of() inside across()

title: 4  Making Packages
text:
4.1 Practical steps
A package is just a directory with a structure R enforces strictly enough that library(), devtools::load_all(), and install.packages() can all treat it as a dependency, rather than a pile of scripts you source() and hope don’t collide with each other. Everything about the workflow follows from that one shift.
Four pieces do almost all the work:
In my opinion, while they are required, there is never any reason to open and look at either NAMESPACE or man.
Why go through this instead of just sourcing scripts, which is what the Quarto-notebook workflow was effectively doing: dependency declarations mean you (or anyone else) can tell what a function needs without reading its body; ?function_name becomes real, queryable documentation instead of prose scattered through a notebook; R CMD check is a free, automated correctness pass that catches undeclared dependencies, broken syntax, and inconsistent documentation before they bite you; and the whole thing becomes installable and shareable as a unit, versioned independently of whatever analysis project happens to be using it.
The entire practical workflow reduces to one loop, repeated as you write or change functions:
write function + roxygen comment above it → document() → load_all() to test interactively → check() to validate → repeat.
Everything below is detail on top of that loop.
To use the function create_package() you give it a folder path, and the last component of that path (the folder’s own name) becomes the package name by default. So usethis::create_package(“~/path/to/pkgname”) creates (or uses, if it already exists) a folder called pkgname, and writes Package: pkgname into DESCRIPTION using that same string.
Editing description can be done manually, and a wrong or missing dependency list going unnoticed is exactly the failure mode R CMD check is built to catch. You don’t need to get Imports: right by careful reasoning up front — you need to run check() after changes and let it tell you what’s wrong, which is fast and deterministic rather than something you have to hold in your head.
Use AI to generate the general text correctly.
Also, the attachment package’s attachment::att_amend_desc() scans every R/*.R file for pkg::fun() and rewrites Imports:
@export is what makes it part of the public API; leave it off for internal helpers.
Set the working directory to your new package directory and run…
Run this after any change to a roxygen comment or to which functions exist. It writes man/*.Rd and regenerates NAMESPACE.
This behaves like library(yourpkg) but reads straight from source, so there’s no install step while you’re iterating. Try ?your_function to confirm the help page rendered. Again, requires working directory set, or pass it the path.
Reports ERRORs (broken, must fix), WARNINGs (should fix – often undeclared dependencies or missing docs), and NOTEs (usually minor/stylistic, e.g. “no visible binding for global variable” from tidyverse-style NSE code, which you resolve with utils::globalVariables() or @importFrom rlang .data). For a personal package, ERRORs matter most; NOTEs are often fine to leave.
Worth it once the package has more than a handful of functions you don’t want to silently regress.
This requires Latex or TinyTex.

title: 4  Making Packages
text:
Scaffold the package. Either usethis::create_package("path/to/pkgname") (creates DESCRIPTION, an empty R/, a license stub, etc. in one call), or build the pieces by hand as done for Quick_descriptives – a DESCRIPTION, an R/ folder, and a placeholder NAMESPACE that roxygen2 will overwrite on first document().






Move functions into R/*.R, one file per logical group is a reasonable default (we split Quick_descriptives into crosstabs.R, missingness.R, numeric_summary.R, etc.). Above each function, write a roxygen block:

#' One-line title
#'
#' Longer description if needed.
#'
#' @param data A data frame.
#' @param vars Character vector of variable names.
#' @return What it returns and its shape.
#' @export
my_function <- function(data, vars) { ... }


Namespace every external call explicitly (dplyr::filter(), not bare filter()), and drop any library() calls from inside R/ files entirely – they don’t belong in package code.
Declare dependencies in DESCRIPTION under Imports: (either by hand, or usethis::use_package("dplyr") which edits it for you). Every package you call with :: needs to be listed here.
Generate docs and NAMESPACE:


devtools::document()


Load and test interactively:

devtools::load_all()


Validate with R CMD check:

devtools::check()


(Optional) Add tests:

usethis::use_testthat()
usethis::use_test("my_function")


(Optional) Install it properly once you’re happy with it, so it behaves like any other package outside of load_all():

devtools::install()          # from local source, pass package folder
devtools::install_local(pkg) # or a path/tarball

(Optional) Documentation site. Either keep hand-written Quarto docs alongside the package (as we did with docs/quick_descriptives_demo.qmd), or generate a browsable reference site automatically from the roxygen comments with pkgdown::build_site() (or altdoc, which can target Quarto specifically). A PDF reference manual (the CRAN-style one) is devtools::build_manual(), which requires a working LaTeX installation.



(Optional) Version control and sharing. git init if the folder isn’t already tracked; push to GitHub and others can install with devtools::install_github("you/repo", subdir = "pkgname") if it’s a subdirectory of a larger repo rather than the repo root.

title: 4  Making Packages
text:
4.2 Software requirements

R itself, obviously.
RStudio (or another IDE) – not required, but its “Build” pane and Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+D/L/T shortcuts map directly onto document()/load_all()/test().
devtools, roxygen2, usethis – the whole workflow above leans on these three: install.packages(c("devtools", "roxygen2", "usethis")).
testthat – only if you add tests (usethis::use_testthat() installs/wires it up for you).
LaTeX – only needed for devtools::build_manual() (the PDF reference manual). Not needed for anything else, including CRAN submission checks in general. TinyTeX (tinytex::install_tinytex()) is the lightweight option; MacTeX is the heavier, more reliable fallback on macOS if TinyTeX’s installer is having a bad day.
pkgdown – only if you want an auto-generated HTML reference site instead of (or alongside) hand-written docs.
git – not required for any of the above to work locally, but close to essential if you want history, sharing, or a monorepo with multiple packages in it.

title: 5  Error catching
text:
5.1 tryCatch
Two options worth considering, tryCatch and withCallingHandlers.
This distinction trips people up. tryCatch() exits the protected code when a condition is caught — you can’t go back. withCallingHandlers() handles the condition in place and, for restartable conditions like warnings and messages, execution can continue afterward.
You may also like purrr::possibly and purrr::safely.
tryCatch key arguments:
Whatever the output of the matched condition is what tryCatch returns.
finally always runs, but if it returns code that is always discarded, it’s just a printing tool, or a tool for resetting values or closing connections.
1 / "a"
## Error in 1/"a": non-numeric argument to binary operator

result <- tryCatch(

  {1 / "a"}, # code that might throw a condition

  error = function(e) {
    message("Caught an error: ", 
            conditionMessage(e), # R's error message
            " from ", 
            deparse(conditionCall(e))) # The code you ran
    NA
  },
  warning = function(w) {
    message("Caught a warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
    NULL
  },
  finally = {
    message("This always runs, success or failure")
  }
)
## Caught an error: non-numeric argument to binary operator from 1/"a"
## This always runs, success or failure

result # Here 'result' returns NA, the return value of the error curly brackets. 
## [1] NA
Using finally to reset values.
result <- tryCatch(
  
  {x = 1
  while(x < 10){
    x = x + 1
  }
  x}, 
  
  finally = {message("x resets to 1")
    x = 1
    }
  
  
)
## x resets to 1

x
## [1] 1
result
## [1] 10
When warning = is specified, a warning will stop your code.
result <- tryCatch(
  
  {as.numeric(c("1", "2", "d"))},
  
  warning = function(w){
  message("Regretably, your code has stopped for this warning. \nNow it just returns NA.")
    NA}
  )
## Regretably, your code has stopped for this warning. 
## Now it just returns NA.

result
## [1] NA
When both warning and error are requested, the one that is triggered first is what gets returned.
result <- tryCatch(
  {
    warning("a warning")
    stop("an error")
  },
  error = function(e) "Would have caught the error",
  warning = function(w) "But the warning appeared first"
)

result
## [1] "But the warning appeared first"
Once an error or warning is specified by tryCatch() this over-rides messages generated by the code itself.
tryCatch({
    warning("a warning")
    })

Warning in tryCatchList(expr, classes, parentenv, handlers): a warning

tryCatch({
    warning("a warning")
    }, 
    warning = function(w){
      "Original warning - over-ridden!"
    })

[1] "Original warning - over-ridden!"

title: 5  Error catching
text:
expr =, the code you’re ‘protecting’.

error =, where an error is returned it runs the expression in the error curly brackets.

warning =, likewise, the warning evaluates the result in its curly bracket.

title: 5  Error catching
text:
5.2 purrr::possibly()
purrr::possibly() is an error suppression tool for functions.
It takes a function, and defines an object to return when it errors, rather than returning the error.


safe_log <- 
  purrr::possibly(
    log, # function to make safe
    otherwise = NA_real_ # object to return in place of errors
    )

safe_log(10)
## [1] 2.302585

log("a")
## Error in log("a"): non-numeric argument to mathematical function

safe_log("a")
## [1] NA

Although, the same effect is obtainable with tryCatch().

safe_log <- function(x) {
  tryCatch(
    log(x),
    error = function(e) NA_real_
  )
}

safe_log("a")

[1] NA

title: 5  Error catching
text:
5.3 safely()
This also wraps a function so it does not stop on an error, but instead instead it returns a list containing both the result and the error.
safely also has an otherwise argument that can be specified so the value returned when erroring is not NULL.

safe_log <- purrr::safely(log)

# Error is NULL because there was not an error
safe_log(10)
## $result
## [1] 2.302585
## 
## $error
## NULL

# Now, there is an error value, but result is NULL. 
safe_log("a")
## $result
## NULL
## 
## $error
## <simpleError in .Primitive("log")(x, base): non-numeric argument to mathematical function>

title: 6  Loading packages from GitHub
text:
6.1 Creating a link
My packages are typically in a subfolder of the repo, so you need to load the sub-folder specifically.
# Take the link from GitHub - 
# https://github.com/Joeacrowley/Descriptives/tree/main/dtab

# But some bits need removing...

# Remove 'https://github.com/' from the URL. 
"Joeacrowley/Descriptives/tree/main/dtab"
## [1] "Joeacrowley/Descriptives/tree/main/dtab"

# Then remove both 'main' and 'tree':
# - 'tree' is GitHub's web-routing convention, not required here and will cause an error. 
# - 'main' is the branch, required only if you want to specify a branch

dtab_link <- "Joeacrowley/Descriptives/dtab"

# If you wanted to specify branch
"Joeacrowley/Descriptives/dtab@main"
## [1] "Joeacrowley/Descriptives/dtab@main"

# This quiets warnings relating to my Rstudio theme. 
options(cli.ignore_unknown_rstudio_theme = TRUE)

title: 6  Loading packages from GitHub
text:
6.2 Installation with pak
Preferred: pak (faster, better dependency resolution than remotes/devtools, and understands sub-directories natively).
It builds a summary of package dependence and compatability, checks it, then installs.
It works well with:

devtools: pkg-development toolkit. load_all(), document(), check(), test(), build(). For building/testing your own packages.

remotes: lightweight installer for non-CRAN sources — GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, local, URL. install_github() etc. devtools used to bundle this; now imports it. Predates pak. Slower, weaker dep resolution, no conflict pre-check — but still fine, widely used.


# Install package
pak::pkg_install(dtab_link)
## ! Using bundled GitHub PAT. Please add your own PAT using `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()`.
## ℹ Loading metadata database
## ✔ Loading metadata database ... done
## 
## 
## ℹ No downloads are needed
## ✔ 1 pkg + 126 deps: kept 43 [5.8s]
library(dtab)

# Now can call dtab
dtab::make_numeric_summary_table(
  mtcars, 
  outcomes = names(mtcars), 
  statistics = c("min", "mean", "max")
  )

pak may struggle at work, it needs its own metadata service which can be blocked by corporate proxies. Alternatively, use remotes::install_github() or install from a local source.

pak::pkg_install("local::C:/path/to/Descriptives/dtab")


The below might work better at work. The installation itself should be the same, but lacks some of the pak checks.

remotes::install_github("Joeacrowley/Descriptives", subdir = "dtab")
